idiom_name: Boost.Asio async_write/async_read chain on a tcp::socket
implementation_notes: Modern C++ default: Boost.Asio supplies the transport and the completion dispatch, so the forwarder is a small object owning a tcp::socket that serialises a typed message into a buffer and calls asio::async_write, while the receiver is an asio::async_read chain that completes one frame, decodes it and invokes the peer's handler; io_context is the receiver loop, replacing the hand-written receiver thread. Because async_read/async_write guarantee completion of the whole buffer, the framing step reduces to choosing the frame (typically a 4-byte big-endian length plus payload). The classic POSA1 structure - separate forwarder/receiver classes plus an explicit dispatcher - is still justified when the same peer must run over several mechanisms or when a non-Asio transport has to be plugged in.
pitfalls: The buffer must outlive async_write - capture the shared_ptr (or the session object); a dangling buffer is the classic Asio bug.
A completion handler must not run blocking work when io_context is single-threaded, or every other connection starves.
Ignoring the error_code makes a dead peer indistinguishable from an idle one; close the socket and notify the peer on the first failure.

variants.name: Boost.Asio with C++20 stackless coroutines
variants.implementation_notes: On a C++20 toolchain the same two roles become linear coroutines: use_awaitable turns async_read/async_write into co_await expressions, so the receiver is a plain read header / read body / dispatch loop and the forwarder is a co_await write instead of a callback chain. The roles and the framing stay exactly as in the callback variant - what changes is control flow, which removes the nested-handler pyramid and the manual state objects it requires. Prefer this variant when the toolchain is C++20 and readability of the session code matters more than compatibility.
pitfalls: A detached co_spawn erases ownership: the session coroutine must own its socket and state, or a destroyed peer leaves a coroutine writing into freed memory.
use_awaitable reports errors as exceptions, so the coroutine body needs a try/catch at its boundary or the failure disappears into the detached frame.
Cancelling a co_await does not cancel the peer's view of the exchange; decide the disconnect policy before spawning.

variants.name: libzmq/cppzmq message sockets
variants.implementation_notes: Here a messaging library owns the whole mechanism: cppzmq wraps libzmq's socket_t and multipart_t, which already frame, queue and (for some socket types) reconnect messages, so the peer's forwarder becomes a push/pair socket that sends a multipart message and the receiver a loop that receives one; the marshalling role moves out of the forwarder into the codec helper (or into multipart frames). Choose this when the transparency of Forwarder-Receiver is wanted but a hand-written transport is not - especially when several peers or a later fan-out may be added - and note that the message contract, versioning and delivery semantics are still the application's responsibility.
pitfalls: ZeroMQ queues instead of blocking: at the high-water mark messages are dropped (or the sender blocks, depending on socket type), so set the HWM deliberately and decide the overflow policy.
Connecting to a peer that is not up yet 'succeeds' - the send is buffered - so failures surface late; monitor and health-check the socket.
Multipart frames are ordered and framing-safe, but a PAIR socket binds two endpoints only; picking the socket type is picking the topology.
